heading: Interior confirmation hearing (January 2025)
body: North Dakota Governor Doug Burgum's confirmation hearing to head the Department of the Interior was held on January 16, 2025 before the Senate Energy Committee, and was the opening item of Badlands Media's Senate confirmation coverage.[n] Most questioning concerned energy policy, with Republicans focused on land access and Democrats on green solutions.[n] A central topic was "baseload" — the minimum level of electricity demand that must be met consistently over time — and Burgum made clear that while he supports renewable energy, US energy demand cannot be reliably supplied with renewables at present technology levels.[n] Badlands commentary summarized his position as prioritizing reliability and declining to put Americans at risk to pursue green energy policies that do not solve America's energy demand, and described Burgum as calm and credible, with even the most combative Democrats such as Hawaii's [[mazie-hirono|Mazie Hirono]] backing off.[n] Representative [[ryan-zinke|Ryan Zinke]] said on Newsmax that he could not "think of a better individual for interior."[n]

heading: EPA confirmation hearing (January 2025)
body: Energy was also a topic during Zeldin's January 2025 confirmation hearing for administrator of the [[environmental-protection-agency|Environmental Protection Agency]], where Badlands commentary described him as calm and credible under questioning.[n] The broader takeaway offered from that day's hearings was that legislators appeared most concerned with protecting their federal funding and enabling public-private partnerships across sectors.[n]

heading: Confirmation hearing scheduling (January 2025)
body: Badlands Media noted that South Dakota Governor Kristi Noem's confirmation hearing was scheduled for 9:00 AM on January 17, 2025, following the previous day's hearings for Doug Burgum and Lee Zeldin.[n]

heading: January 2025 Trump cabinet hearings
body:
The January 2025 round of confirmation hearings for Donald Trump's second-term cabinet drew commentary on both preparation and partisanship.[n] Representative [[ryan-zinke|Ryan Zinke]] told Newsmax that Trump's slate was "enormously talented" and "very well prepared," claiming the nominees were better prepared on policy than some Democratic senators questioning them.[n] Badlands coverage of [[doug-burgum|Doug Burgum]]'s Senate Energy Committee hearing found Republicans focused on land access and Democrats on green solutions, with baseload electricity demand the central technical dispute, and reported that [[lee-zeldin|Lee Zeldin]]'s EPA hearing was similarly energy-focused.[n] The overall takeaway offered was that legislators were most concerned with protecting federal funding streams and enabling public-private partnerships in every sector.[n]

A parallel controversy concerned Democratic questioning about whether Donald Trump "lost" the 2020 election.[n] The Federalist argued that the query includes an undefined term — "lost" — carrying different meanings for Trump supporters and for anti-Trump questioners: if "lost" merely meant that Joe Biden became president, the answer is straightforward, and nominee Pam Bondi repeatedly and expressly attested that Biden is the president of the United States.[n] What senators such as Dick Durbin and Richard Blumenthal sought, the argument ran, was a concession that Trump's election challenges were frivolous, unfounded, or wrong, a meaning Democrats inject into the word "lost" — as the legacy media had earlier done in hounding then-Senator [[jd-vance|J.D. Vance]].[n]

heading: Ohio Senate seat appointment push (January 2025)
body: In January 2025, President-elect Donald Trump encouraged Ramaswamy to consider filling Ohio's vacant Senate seat should the post be offered to him, according to two people with knowledge of private deliberations.[n] Ramaswamy had publicly withdrawn his name from consideration in November 2024 after Trump chose him to lead the Department of Government Efficiency panel alongside [[elon-musk|Elon Musk]], but the Ohio native reemerged as one of the leading contenders and entered advanced discussions with GOP leaders about the position.[n] The seat became vacant when [[jd-vance|JD Vance]] resigned to serve as Trump's vice president; under Ohio law Governor [[mike-dewine|Mike DeWine]] appoints a replacement for the next two years, with a special election on November 3, 2026 deciding who serves until the term expires in 2029.[n] While the decision rested with DeWine, Trump personally appealed to Ramaswamy to accept the appointment if offered.[n] Badlands contributor Chris Paul was dismissive, characterizing Ramaswamy's qualifications as saying nice things online, attending a few rallies, and being a close friend of JD Vance and his wife.[n]

heading: Ohio Senate vacancy (January 2025)
body: Following [[jd-vance|JD Vance]]'s resignation from the Senate to become vice president, Ohio law placed the appointment of his replacement with Governor DeWine, who would name a successor to serve for the next two years before a special election on November 3, 2026 determines who holds the seat until the term expires in 2029.[n] In January 2025 [[vivek-ramaswamy|Vivek Ramaswamy]] emerged as a leading contender and entered advanced discussions with GOP leaders, with President-elect Donald Trump personally appealing to him to accept the appointment if DeWine offered it.[n]
